newsitem.title: USA: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS - LEAPS grab the spotlight.
newsitem.headline: U.S. OPTIONS FOCUS - LEAPS grab the spotlight.

text.p: Long-term options, commonly called LEAPS (long-term equity anticipation securities), dominated individual equity options trading Tuesday, traders said.
LEAPS on shares of International Business Machines Corp, Time Warner Inc, Telebras and Philip Morris Cos Inc were among the busiest options around.
For IBM, several January 1998 calls and puts were busy as the underlying shares flirted with historic highs. In late trade, IBM was up 1-3/4 at 175-1/4 after hitting 177-1/8.
The IBM January 1998 190 call traded 2,580 contracts and the 180 call traded 2,413. On the put side, the January 1998 140 put traded 2,109 contracts and the 170 put traded 1,992.
Jon Najarian, president of Mercury Trading, the designated primary market maker for IBM options, said an investor sold 2,000 of the January 1998 140 puts to the trading crowd.
"Somebody was just trying to squeeze out a little more premium for themselves," he said. A block of 2,000 of the January 1998 140 puts crossed at 2-3/8.
"It was probably someone who owns stock and is just writing (the options) against it," Najarian said.
In Time Warner LEAPS, the January 1999 40 put traded 6,325 contracts and the January 1999 55 call traded 7,425.
The stock was up 1-3/8 at 46-3/8.

Michael Schwartz, a managing director at Oppenheimer & Co, said the activity in the Time Warner LEAPS could be a collar, with an investor buying the out-of-the-money 40 puts and selling the out-of-the-money 55 calls.
The puts went out at two and the calls went out at prices ranging from 2-9/16 to 3-1/8.
The investor could have used the proceeds from selling the calls to buy the puts.

Buying the 40 puts would give the investor the option of selling Time Warner shares at 40 if they broke below that level. Selling the 55 calls would mean the investor would have to sell the stock at 55 if it climbed past that level and the call buyer exercised.
The LEAPS activity in Telebras appeared to be an investor rolling a position up to a higher strike price, traders said.
The Telebras January 1998 115 call traded 7,755 contracts and the 125 call traded 7,750. The January 1999 115 and 125 call each traded 10,000 contracts.
"It looks to me like someone sold the 115s and bought the 125s," said Harrison Roth, a first vice president at Cowen & Co in New York.
Open interest in the January 1998 115 call was 9,937 and in the 125 call was 6,876. In the January 1999 115 call, open ineterst was 11,278 and in the 125 call was 2,349.
American Depositary Receipts of Telebras fell 1-1/4 to 126 but not before reaching a record intraday high of 128-1/4. The stock has been on a strong upswing recently.
In Philip Morris LEAPS, the January 1999 36-5/8 put traded 7,105 contracts. It had open interest of 2,010 contracts.
